title: Spatial symmetry invariance of three-dimensional Navier-Stokes turbulence
authors: Shijun Liao
abstract: Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) of the deterministic Navier-Stokes (NS) equations is widely used to provide benchmark solutions of turbulent flow, but its accuracy and reliability have not been rigorously inspected from a mathematical viewpoint. Here we prove a spatial symmetry invariance theorem (SSIT) of three-dimensional NS equations whereby an exact solution of deterministic NS equations under periodic boundary conditions maintains the same spatial symmetry as its symmetric initial flow, forever. SSIT provides an absolute benchmark test for computational fluid dynamics (CFD). It is shown herein that traditional DNS of NS turbulence quickly violates SSIT, revealing that the spatiotemporal trajectory of NS turbulence predicted by DNS soon becomes badly polluted by numerical noise. Importantly, it is found that even the statistical results of DNS might be unstable, i.e., exhibit sensitivity dependence on the initial flow conditions. In other words, the loss of spatial symmetry in traditional DNS of NS turbulence is not a physical instability but instead a numerical artifact caused by the chaotic nature of the flow. Using the SSIT, it is straightforward to deduce several key properties of NS turbulence, including `ultra-chaos', the so-called `noise-expansion cascade', `permanent memory of symmetric initial flow conditions', and so on. Note that permanent memory of symmetric initial flow conditions suggests that NS turbulence governed by deterministic NS equations subject to symmetric initial flow should have no `mixing', corresponding to non-ergodicity, although ergodicity is one of the most fundamental assumptions of turbulence theory.

infographic.key_insight: The paper presents a spatial symmetry invariance theorem stating that exact three-dimensional Navier–Stokes solutions preserve symmetric initial-flow structure under periodic boundary conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Symmetry preservation offers a benchmark for detecting numerical contamination in turbulence simulations used for CFD validation.
method: Derive a spatial symmetry invariance theorem for deterministic Navier–Stokes equations.
Test traditional DNS against the predicted symmetry preservation.
Examine implications for statistical sensitivity and memory of initial conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports rapid symmetry loss in traditional DNS and possible sensitivity of turbulence statistics to initial conditions, but provides no quantitative errors or simulation details.
infographic.watch_item: Symmetry loss can flag numerical error, but claims about statistical unreliability and non-ergodicity require scrutiny beyond this symmetry benchmark.
infographic.paper_title: Spatial symmetry invariance of three-dimensional Navier-Stokes turbulence

title: Generative AI in Turbulence: Foundations, Applications, Validations and Benchmarks
authors: Luca Biferale, Michele Buzzicotti
abstract: Generative AI offers new approaches to turbulence problems in which incomplete observations or unresolved d.o.f. admit multiple physically plausible solutions. Potential applications include stochastic closures, super-resolution, data assimilation, uncertainty quantification, and the generation of Eulerian and Lagrangian flow ensembles. However, turbulence is not a conventional image-generation problem. Its multiscale dynamics, intermittency, extreme events, rough velocity fields and intrinsically stochastic transport make visual realism, pointwise error, and low-order spectral agreement insufficient measures of physical fidelity. We examine where generative AI provide novel capabilities with emphasis on diffusion models, score-based methods, and related probability-transport formulations. We discuss their use in unconditional generation, probabilistic reconstruction, reduced-order modeling, temporal evolution, and mesh-free representations. We argue that validation must address turbulence properties: energy transfer, structure functions, anomalous scaling, pdf tails, coherent structures, conservation laws, temporal consistency, ensemble diversity and generalization. Finally, we discuss potential limitations in validation, baseline, data availability and reproducibility, and the need for a benchmark ecosystem combining open data, standardized challenges, hidden tests, physics-aware metrics, and documented failures. This paper serves as a bridge between two communities. For AI practitioners, we provide a fair and accessible introduction to turbulence, essential for appreciating the challenges posed by the field and for assessing the physical relevance of generative models. For turbulent practitioners, we provide an introduction to the key technological aspects of Generative AI, clarifying what these tools actually do, and where their potential and current limitations lie.

infographic.key_insight: Generative AI can produce multiple plausible turbulent-flow solutions, but physical fidelity requires validation beyond visual realism, pointwise error, and low-order spectra.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Potential engineering applications include stochastic closures, flow super-resolution, data assimilation, and uncertainty quantification when observations or resolved scales are incomplete.
method: Reviews diffusion, score-based, and related probability-transport methods for turbulence.
Examines flow generation, probabilistic reconstruction, reduced-order modeling, and temporal evolution.
Proposes physics-aware validation and an open, standardized benchmark ecosystem.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract outlines evaluation priorities—including energy transfer, intermittency, conservation, temporal consistency, and ensemble diversity—rather than reporting quantitative model performance.
infographic.watch_item: Limited data, weak baselines, and incomplete physical validation may undermine claims of generalization and reproducibility.
infographic.paper_title: Generative AI in Turbulence: Foundations, Applications, Validations and Benchmarks

title: Toward fully stabilized flow control using deep reinforcement learning
authors: Wang Jia, Hang Xu
abstract: This study enhances the performance of flow control across various synthetic jet configurations by improving deep reinforcement learning techniques. The training results based on the foundational deep reinforcement learning framework indicate that as the Reynolds number increases, the effectiveness of synthetic jet control becomes increasingly sensitive to the position of the jet. When synthetic jets are positioned near the flow separation region, the control strategy consistently exhibits excellent performance. However, when synthetic jets are located farther from the separation region, the flow control performance diminishes, and the consumption of external energy increases. By enhancing dynamic state features and reshaping the reward function, we significantly improve control performance across various Reynolds numbers and synthetic jet positions. With the optimized framework, we achieve significant drag reduction effects ranging from 8% to 34% within the Reynolds number range of 100 to 400. The flow control strategy is capable of simultaneously achieving multiple control objectives, including reducing drag, suppressing lift, eliminating vortex shedding, and decreasing energy consumption. These findings highlight the potential of optimizing deep reinforcement learning frameworks to achieve more adaptive flow control strategies for various flow scenarios.

infographic.key_insight: Enhanced state features and reward shaping improve deep reinforcement learning flow control across synthetic jet positions, achieving 8–34% drag reduction at Reynolds numbers of 100–400.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More adaptive synthetic jet control could reduce drag and energy use while suppressing lift fluctuations and vortex shedding.
method: Train deep reinforcement learning controllers across Reynolds numbers and synthetic jet positions.
Enhance dynamic state features to improve flow-state representation.
Reshape rewards to balance multiple flow-control objectives.

infographic.paper_title: Toward fully stabilized flow control using deep reinforcement learning

title: From Stochastic Transport Models to High-Dimensional Bayesian Inference
authors: Dan Crisan, Oana Lang
abstract: The Stochastic Transport in Upper Ocean Dynamics project introduced a new paradigm for representing uncertainty in geophysical fluid dynamics through stochastic transport models calibrated from data. This paper provides a synthesis of the principal theoretical and data assimilation developments achieved as part of the project. The central theme of the paper is the transformation of stochastic transport models from a modelling paradigm into a mathematically rigorous framework equipped with analytical, variational, calibration and Bayesian data assimilation methodologies suitable for geophysical fluid dynamics. We describe the development of the theory of stochastic transport equations, including well-posedness, regularity and approximation results, together with their geometric foundations based on stochastic variational principles, rough paths and fractional transport models. We further review methodologies for calibrating stochastic transport structures from observational and high-resolution simulation data, ranging from reduced-order stochastic models to modern generative approaches. Finally, we discuss Bayesian inference and high-dimensional data assimilation techniques developed for stochastic transport models, including particle filter methodologies and machine learning uncertainty quantification. Taken together, these developments establish a coherent framework linking stochastic transport modelling, rigorous analysis, calibration and Bayesian inference, thereby providing a foundation for uncertainty quantification and forecasting in geophysical fluid dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Stochastic transport models connect uncertainty-aware geophysical fluid dynamics with rigorous analysis, data-driven calibration and high-dimensional Bayesian inference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports uncertainty quantification and forecasting for ocean and other geophysical flows.
method: Develop well-posedness, regularity and approximation theory for stochastic transport equations.
Calibrate stochastic transport structures using observations and high-resolution simulations.
Apply Bayesian data assimilation, particle filters and machine-learning uncertainty quantification.

infographic.watch_item: Practical scalability and forecasting accuracy in high-dimensional applications are not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: From Stochastic Transport Models to High-Dimensional Bayesian Inference

title: State-augmented deep reinforcement learning for active flow control around an elliptical cylinder
authors: Wang Jia, Hang Xu
abstract: We employ reinforcement learning algorithms to develop control strategies for manipulating synthetic jets on an elliptical cylinder, targeting robust flow control across varying aspect ratios (Ar). Our results show that for high aspect ratios (Ar = 1 and 0.75), the learned strategies effectively mitigate vortex shedding, achieving drag reductions of 13.4% and 20.1%, respectively. As the Ar decreases, more complex wake dynamics challenge flow control. For Ar = 0.5 and 0.25, drag reductions of 26.88% and 30.37% are achieved, though vortex suppression becomes increasingly difficult. For extremely slender cylinders (Ar = 0.1), we enhance control performance by enriching dynamic feature representation and using Kalman filtering for state estimation. Unlike conventional methods, our approach successfully achieves complete vortex shedding suppression, a maximum drag reduction of 32.2%, and eliminates periodic oscillations, stabilizing the flow. These results demonstrate the efficacy of state-enhanced RL in controlling highly slender geometries.

infographic.key_insight: State-augmented reinforcement learning controls synthetic jets around elliptical cylinders, achieving complete vortex-shedding suppression and up to 32.2% drag reduction at aspect ratio Ar = 0.1.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a path to reducing drag and stabilizing wakes around slender bodies with challenging flow dynamics.
method: Learn synthetic-jet actuation strategies using deep reinforcement learning.
Evaluate flow control across elliptical-cylinder aspect ratios.

infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish net energy savings after accounting for synthetic-jet actuation costs.
infographic.paper_title: State-augmented deep reinforcement learning for active flow control around an elliptical cylinder

title: Solving and Learning Navier-Stokes Dynamics with the Neural Basis Method
authors: Yuhe Wang, Zhu Wang, Min Wang
abstract: Physics-informed machine learning has become a major direction in predictive modeling of fluid dynamics, combining governing physics with learned representations. Yet prevailing formulations neither guarantee that small PDE-residual losses imply small solution errors nor scale effectively with increasing problem size. Here we present the neural basis method (NBM) as a new approach for Navier--Stokes dynamics. NBM is built on a ``representation-then-projection'' principle: fixed neural bases define the representation space, while projection of the governing equations determines the expansion coefficients. The same bases define common coordinates for the parametric solution manifold, recasting operator learning as a parameter-to-coefficient mapping and enabling scalability by removing explicit spatial dependence. For incompressible flow, NBM yields a velocity-only formulation whose residual provides an a posteriori velocity-error estimate, establishing a certified, data-free training objective for coefficient learning. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, generalization, and scalability of NBM, with substantial improvements over baselines.

infographic.key_insight: The neural basis method separates fixed neural representations from physics-based coefficient determination to solve and learn Navier–Stokes dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shared basis coordinates can make parametric flow prediction more scalable by learning parameter-to-coefficient maps rather than spatially dependent solution maps.
method: Represent flow solutions with fixed neural bases.
Project governing equations to determine expansion coefficients.
For incompressible flow, use a velocity-only residual that provides an a posteriori velocity-error estimate for data-free coefficient learning.

infographic.watch_item: Practical performance depends on whether the fixed neural basis adequately represents the target flow regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Solving and Learning Navier-Stokes Dynamics with the Neural Basis Method

title: Physics-Constrained Symbolic Regression for Mean-Velocity and Mixing-Length Scaling in Zero-Pressure-Gradient Turbulent Boundary Layers
authors: Xianglin Shan, Weiwei Zhang
abstract: Developing interpretable full-profile relations for mean velocity and effective mixing length remains challenging because the near-wall, overlap, and outer regions exhibit distinct scaling behaviors. In this paper, physics-constrained symbolic regression is used to construct analytical relations for incompressible zero-pressure-gradient turbulent boundary layers. Classical logarithmic and Prandtl mixing-length scalings provide the starting points, while the regression identifies near-wall transition functions under asymptotic constraints and Reynolds-number-dependent outer corrections. The resulting expressions retain the prescribed leading-order near-wall exponents, reproduce the principal overlap-region behavior, and describe finite-Reynolds-number variations. The mean-velocity relation agrees well with 35 profiles from direct numerical simulations, large-eddy simulations, and experiments spanning friction Reynolds numbers from 252 to 72,526, while the mixing-length relation captures the principal trends in the simulation-derived data. These results illustrate how physical scaling knowledge can guide symbolic regression toward compact, interpretable analytical descriptions of canonical wall turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-constrained symbolic regression yields compact, interpretable relations for mean velocity and effective mixing length across zero-pressure-gradient turbulent boundary layers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These relations could support engineering estimates of boundary-layer profiles while preserving key physical scaling behavior.
method: Start from classical logarithmic and Prandtl mixing-length scalings.
Identify near-wall transition functions under prescribed asymptotic constraints.
Add Reynolds-number-dependent outer corrections.

infographic.watch_item: Applicability beyond incompressible zero-pressure-gradient boundary layers is not established by the reported evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-Constrained Symbolic Regression for Mean-Velocity and Mixing-Length Scaling in Zero-Pressure-Gradient Turbulent Boundary Layers

title: Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI
authors: Jiawei Chen, Xiang I. A. Yang, Ping He
abstract: Traditional turbulence-model development relies heavily on expert knowledge and is time-consuming. This study develops an agentic AI framework, DEScover (automated Discovery of DES closures), to explore subgrid length scales for detached eddy simulation (DES). The user provides only a modeling idea: the length scale is the grid width normal to the local vortex axis. Four large language model (LLM) agents then propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate formulations and generate scripts for CFD simulations. The Discovery Agent infers the vortex axis from various vortex-identification methods. The candidates are tested on four cases spanning canonical and engineering flows: a flat plate, a backward-facing step, a free shear layer, and an iced airfoil. For all test cases, the best candidate consistently outperforms the standard length scale based on the maximum cell size. Its accuracy is similar to, or slightly better than, that of the expert-designed shear-layer-adapted length scale. Each agentic discovery run takes about 25 minutes on average, excluding the CFD simulations. These results show that LLM-based reasoning can significantly accelerate the discovery of physically interpretable turbulence models and reduce reliance on manual expert formulation.

infographic.key_insight: DEScover uses four LLM agents to discover physically interpretable DES subgrid length scales from the idea of measuring grid width normal to the local vortex axis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could accelerate turbulence-model development while improving DES accuracy relative to the standard maximum-cell-size length scale.
method: Infer local vortex axes using candidate vortex-identification methods.
Use four agents to propose, review, implement, and evaluate length-scale formulations.
Generate CFD simulation scripts to test candidate closures.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across flat-plate, backward-facing-step, free-shear-layer, and iced-airfoil tests, the best candidate consistently outperformed the standard length scale and matched or slightly exceeded an expert-designed shear-layer-adapted scale.

infographic.paper_title: Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI

title: Flow Mesh: A Velocity-Regularized Flow Matching Framework for Stable Distributional Modeling of Physical Fields on Unstructured Meshes
authors: Siddharth Verma, Jaewan Park, Jay Phil Yoo, Kazuma Kobayashi, Souvik Chakraborty, Syed Bahauddin Alam
abstract: Thermal-fluid field distributions underpin the analysis and operation of energy infrastructure, from nuclear-reactor cooling channels to industrial heat exchangers, but resolving these distributions through computational fluid dynamics requires prohibitively large simulation ensembles. Their complex geometries also demand unstructured meshes that are poorly accommodated by generative models developed for regular grids. Here we introduce FlowMesh, a generative framework that combines permutation-invariant mesh encoding with deterministic latent flow matching and an l1 penalty on the learned transport velocity. FlowMesh generates full-field realizations directly on fixed unstructured meshes without auxiliary grid interpolation or a stochastic denoising chain. Across lid-driven-cavity, pressurized-water-reactor subchannel and heat-exchanger datasets, evaluated over six matched training seeds, FlowMesh achieves macro-averaged probability-density-function coverage of 91.7%-97.0%, exceeding an architecture-controlled latent diffusion model by $11.6$--$45.4$ percentage points. Latent-velocity regularization increases coverage by $3.8$ percentage points for reactor flows and 1.1 points for heat-exchanger flows, while reducing temperature-field Kullback--Leibler divergence by 1.7-2.4-fold. Each full-field realization requires 1.23 \pm 0.15 s, providing a 585--1902-fold wall-clock acceleration over computational fluid dynamics. FlowMesh therefore makes large-scale generative characterization of thermal-fluid states computationally feasible, providing a foundation for data-driven analysis and digital-twin development in fixed-geometry energy systems.

infographic.key_insight: FlowMesh generates thermal-fluid fields directly on unstructured meshes, improving distributional coverage over latent diffusion while accelerating generation relative to CFD.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fast full-field sampling could support uncertainty analysis and digital twins for fixed-geometry reactor cooling channels and heat exchangers.
method: Permutation-invariant encoding of unstructured meshes.
Deterministic latent flow matching without grid interpolation or stochastic denoising.
L1 regularization of learned transport velocity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three datasets and six matched training seeds, FlowMesh achieved 91.7–97.0% macro-averaged PDF coverage, outperforming architecture-controlled latent diffusion by 11.6–45.4 percentage points, with 585–1902× wall-clock speedups over CFD.
infographic.watch_item: The reported results concern fixed unstructured meshes; transfer to new geometries and enforcement of physical conservation require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Flow Mesh: A Velocity-Regularized Flow Matching Framework for Stable Distributional Modeling of Physical Fields on Unstructured Meshes

title: Neural Eigenfluid Bases: Spectral Objectives, Gauge, and Topology
authors: Baiming Zhang, Shiying Xiong, Zhecheng Wang
abstract: Reduced-order models simplify fluid simulation by representing complex flows with a small number of spatial modes. Building on Laplacian Eigenfluids, we introduce Neural Eigenfluid Bases (NEB), a neural representation whose basis functions can be evaluated anywhere in space. We enforce incompressibility and impermeable boundaries directly through differential lifts and potential boundary conditions. Geometry-local orthogonalization and Rayleigh minimization then learn an ordered basis. We connect learning in potential and velocity spaces, and derive a spectral-variance relation explaining why these objectives weight approximate modes differently, even though their exact positive spectra agree. Gauge fixing reduces the number of spatial derivatives needed for potential learning, while a Dirichlet energy loss learns independent circulation fields around obstacles. With 1024 modes, both objectives keep velocity errors below 1% in periodic vortex merger. For random flows around obstacles, potential-based learning captures more initial energy and gives lower final errors than numerical Laplacian bases of the same size. The reduced state is about a thousand times smaller than the full reference model. Three-dimensional tests separate spatial reconstruction errors from errors in coefficient evolution. Precomputed Galerkin operators allow millisecond-scale updates when the same basis is reused across simulations. This provides a physically constrained basis for continuous flow reconstruction and efficient reduced-order simulation.

infographic.key_insight: Neural Eigenfluid Bases learn spatially continuous, ordered flow modes that enforce incompressibility and impermeable boundaries while supporting compact reduced-order simulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reusing a learned basis with precomputed Galerkin operators enables millisecond-scale updates and a reduced state about 1,000 times smaller than the full reference model.
method: Enforce physical constraints through differential lifts and potential boundary conditions.
Learn ordered modes using geometry-local orthogonalization and Rayleigh minimization, with gauge fixing to reduce derivative requirements.
Learn independent circulation fields around obstacles using a Dirichlet energy loss.
infographic.evidence_signal: With 1,024 modes, both learning objectives keep periodic vortex-merger velocity errors below 1%; potential-based learning also captures more initial energy and yields lower final errors than same-size numerical Laplacian bases for random obstacle flows.
infographic.watch_item: Millisecond-scale updates depend on basis reuse and precomputed operators; coefficient-evolution errors remain distinct from spatial reconstruction errors.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Eigenfluid Bases: Spectral Objectives, Gauge, and Topology

title: When does boundary-condition uncertainty outweigh thermal and vegetation effects in street canyon flow? A global sensitivity analysis of input uncertainty
authors: Albert Moreno Català, Joan Calafell Sandiumenge, Nikolaj T. Mücke, Jan Mateu Armengol
abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is increasingly used to resolve wind, heat, and pollution patterns in cities with high fidelity but high computational cost. Thermal effects and vegetation are often neglected despite being important drivers, yet their influence may be masked by variability from other uncertain inputs. This work determines how precisely model parameters and boundary conditions must be known for these effects to govern output uncertainty in the velocity, temperature, and concentration fields of a two-dimensional street canyon. A global Sobol analysis of 24 parameters is made tractable by a surrogate trained on Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) simulations, combining principal component analysis (PCA) with multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Two ventilation regimes assess the variance due to thermal and vegetation parameters as uncertainty in all other inputs is progressively reduced. At typical uncertainty levels, turbulence closure constants and inflow turbulence profiles govern variability in all three fields in both regimes. Under weak ventilation, solar forcing becomes the main source of temperature variability once the remaining uncertainties are halved, and of concentration variance once they are reduced to a quarter (about $\pm11\%$ for the dominant closure constant and $\pm12\%$ for the emission rate). In contrast, vegetation contributes significantly at typical uncertainty levels. Under strong ventilation, however, the canopy never overtakes the closure constants, even when the dominant one is known to $\pm5\%$. Spatially, both effects peak at road level and along canyon walls, which influence outdoor exposure and indoor infiltration, suggesting that high-resolution exposure studies should account for them.

infographic.key_insight: Turbulence closure and inflow uncertainty generally dominate street-canyon predictions, but reducing other uncertainties reveals solar effects under weak ventilation, while vegetation already contributes significantly at typical uncertainty levels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Urban exposure studies should constrain turbulence and boundary-condition inputs while resolving thermal and vegetation effects near roads and canyon walls.
method: Run RANS simulations of a two-dimensional street canyon in two ventilation regimes.
Train a PCA–multilayer-perceptron surrogate for velocity, temperature, and concentration fields.
Apply global Sobol analysis to 24 uncertain inputs while progressively narrowing nonthermal, nonvegetation uncertainties.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under weak ventilation, solar forcing dominates temperature variance when other uncertainties are halved and concentration variance when quartered; under strong ventilation, canopy effects never exceed closure-constant effects, even with the dominant constant constrained to ±5%.
infographic.watch_item: The thresholds come from a surrogate-assisted, two-dimensional RANS study and may not transfer directly to three-dimensional urban geometries.
infographic.paper_title: When does boundary-condition uncertainty outweigh thermal and vegetation effects in street canyon flow? A global sensitivity analysis of input uncertainty

title: Physics Informed Neural Network for Multi-dimensional Turbulent Self-gravitating Flows
authors: Tirthankar De, Sayantan Auddy, Ramit Dey, Shantanu Basu
abstract: Molecular clouds exhibit complex, multi-scale dynamics driven by the interplay of turbulence, self-gravity, and gas pressure. Modelling these systems with conventional grid-based methods becomes increasingly expensive as spatial resolution and dimensionality increase. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative by incorporating the governing equations directly into the training objective, but their ability to model realistic turbulent self-gravitating flows remains largely unexplored. We apply PINNs to isothermal molecular clouds initialized with astrophysically motivated turbulent velocity fields, considering subsonic and supersonic evolution in two and three dimensions. We benchmark the predicted density and velocity fields against the finite-volume code Athena++. PINNs accurately recover the global evolution of the flow over multiple free-fall times across turbulent realizations, Mach numbers, and dimensionalities. Their training cost also exhibits weak dependence on spatial resolution, increasing by less than 25% from 128^3 to 1024^3 in our experiments. These results demonstrate that PINNs can model substantially more realistic self-gravitating turbulent flows than previously explored and provide a promising complementary framework for studying these systems.

infographic.key_insight: PINNs reproduce the global evolution of turbulent, self-gravitating molecular clouds in 2D and 3D while showing weak training-cost dependence on spatial resolution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This mesh-free approach offers a promising complement to grid-based simulation for computationally demanding, multiscale compressible flows with self-gravity.
method: Embed governing physics in the neural-network training objective.
Model isothermal clouds initialized with astrophysically motivated turbulence.
Benchmark density and velocity predictions against Athena++ finite-volume simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports accurate global evolution over multiple free-fall times across turbulent realizations, subsonic and supersonic regimes, and dimensionalities, with training cost rising less than 25% from 128³ to 1024³.
infographic.watch_item: Global agreement and weak resolution-dependent training cost do not alone establish accuracy for shocks or small-scale structure, or an absolute speed advantage over Athena++.
infographic.paper_title: Physics Informed Neural Network for Multi-dimensional Turbulent Self-gravitating Flows

title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks
authors: Takeru Hasegawa, Naoto Mitsume, Shota Deguchi, Mitsuteru Asai, Tetsuya Kanagawa
abstract: Interactions between ultrasound and microbubbles underlie a range of biomedical and industrial applications, yet predicting how the physical parameters of the medium and bubbles govern nonlinear wave propagation remains difficult. This study proposes a parameter estimation framework that combines a Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers (KdVB) equation, describing weakly nonlinear wave propagation in a bubbly liquid, with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). The contributions are threefold. First, the PINN reproduces the reference solution of the governing equation in the forward problem, with a near-zero prediction error at the initial time that confirms the initial condition is enforced exactly as intended. Second, prior to inverse estimation, a sensitivity analysis is introduced that quantifies, at both the coefficient and solution levels, how each of eight physical parameters influences the KdVB equation, allowing the expected difficulty of estimating each parameter to be assessed in advance. Third, based on this assessment, single-parameter inverse estimation is performed for seven of the eight parameters using the PINN. Liquid viscosity, bubble initial radius, liquid density, sound speed, and liquid pressure are estimated with errors of 0.8-2.1%, the polytropic exponent converges only partially, and the surface tension coefficient cannot be estimated at all, consistent with the sensitivity analysis. These results establish a general framework for identifying and estimating the physical parameters governing nonlinear wave propagation in bubbly liquids from observed waveform data.

infographic.key_insight: Sensitivity analysis helps anticipate which bubbly-liquid parameters a physics-informed neural network can recover from nonlinear waveforms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support characterization of bubbly media for ultrasound applications by identifying parameters that measurably influence wave propagation.
method: Model weakly nonlinear propagation with a Korteweg–de Vries–Burgers equation.
Assess eight physical parameters through coefficient- and solution-level sensitivity analyses.
Use a PINN for forward prediction and single-parameter inverse estimation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across seven single-parameter inverse tests, five parameters were estimated within 0.8–2.1% error; the polytropic exponent converged partially, while surface tension could not be estimated.
infographic.watch_item: Single-parameter results do not establish reliable joint estimation of multiple parameters, especially those with weak waveform sensitivity.
infographic.paper_title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks

title: Let's Do Turbulence Right: In Space and Time!
authors: Maximilian Plattner, Fabian Paischer, Johannes Brandstetter
abstract: The three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations govern fluid turbulence, a chaotic and non-linear physical phenomenon characterized by complex eddies interacting across vast spatial and temporal scales. A numerically accurate modeling of this multi-scale energy cascade requires fully resolving both the fine spatial structures and the continuous temporal evolution of the flow field. In this paper, we leverage massive, time-resolved direct numerical simulations, which exceed 28 TB per run, to assess how numerical choices govern the resolved (3+1)-dimensional physics of turbulent flows. Building on this analysis, we study how neural networks represent the recorded turbulent motion. Our results highlight that spatial and temporal assessments can disagree for both numerical records and learned representations. We therefore call on the machine learning community to treat (3+1)-dimensional turbulence as a four-dimensional phenomenon.

infographic.key_insight: Turbulence must be assessed jointly in space and time, because spatial and temporal evaluations can disagree for both numerical simulations and neural representations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable AI-based turbulence modeling requires validation of both fine-scale flow structures and temporal evolution, not spatial accuracy alone.
method: Analyze massive, time-resolved direct numerical simulations.
Assess how numerical choices affect resolved space–time turbulence.
Study neural network representations of the recorded flow.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study uses direct numerical simulations exceeding 28 TB per run and reports disagreement between spatial and temporal assessments.
infographic.watch_item: Fully resolved space–time data impose substantial storage and computational demands; the abstract does not quantify neural model accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Let's Do Turbulence Right: In Space and Time!

title: Microscopic Derivation of Stochastic Thin-Film Equation and Extensions to Two-Layer and Evaporating Films
authors: Toby Kay, Serafim Kalliadasis
abstract: While classical thin-film hydrodynamics models widely govern macroscopic fluid layers, they fail to capture the molecular-level thermal fluctuations that dictate nanoscale interfacial dynamics. Standard stochastic extensions rely on the long-wave approximation of the continuum fluctuating Navier-Stokes equations; however, this top-down paradigm lacks a formal connection to microscopic particle trajectories and cannot readily accommodate complex, non-equilibrium boundary mechanisms. We resolve this limitation by deriving the stochastic thin-film equation directly from the exact underlying N-particle Hamiltonian dynamics. This is achieved via a systematic, bottom-up coarse-graining framework based on a generalized fluctuating dynamic density-functional theory. Crucially, this first principles formulation offers unparalleled flexibility, enabling the seamless integration of multi-layered interfaces and non-conserved dynamics such as evaporation. For these complex configurations, our framework rigorously yields entirely novel stochastic thin-film equations featuring emergent noise terms that encapsulate microscopic fluctuations missing from classical top-down models.

infographic.key_insight: Deriving stochastic thin-film equations directly from N-particle Hamiltonian dynamics reveals microscopic noise contributions for two-layer and evaporating films.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could improve nanoscale coating and evaporating-film models where thermal fluctuations and coupled interfaces matter.
method: Start from exact microscopic N-particle Hamiltonian dynamics.
Coarse-grain using generalized fluctuating dynamic density-functional theory.
Extend the derivation to two-layer interfaces and non-conserved evaporation dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical derivations of new stochastic equations but provides no numerical benchmarks or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Practical accuracy and computational cost for specific materials and evaporation conditions remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Microscopic Derivation of Stochastic Thin-Film Equation and Extensions to Two-Layer and Evaporating Films

title: A Priori Estimation of the Non-Linear Compression Potential and Quantification of Autoencoder Non-Linearity in Turbulent Flows
authors: Niklas Alexander Pissarski, Juan Pablo Murcia Leon, Søren Juhl Andersen
abstract: Data-driven reduced-order modelling (ROM) of turbulent flows is based on an efficient and physical low-dimensional representation of the flow process. Such a dimension reduction can be achieved using proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) or non-linear autoencoders. Capturing the inherent non-linearities in turbulent flows offers the potential for improved compression rates. This work proposes the local tangent residual (LTR) as an a priori estimate of the potential benefit of non-linear dimension reduction for a given dataset. The LTR is based on the local geometry of the data points, requiring neither prior model training nor the definition of a threshold parameter. For all datasets investigated in this work, namely, two vortex street cases and the turbulent wake flow of a wind turbine, the dominant trends in autoencoder compression performance are reproduced by the proposed LTR. The results are further contextualised through the decoder linearisation error (DLE). The DLE quantifies the non-linearity of the trained decoder by comparing it to a linearised surrogate model, which enables physical interpretability of the non-linearities. Together, a large non-linear compression potential in the turbulent flow, as quantified by the LTR, is corroborated by a large DLE, i.e., a pronounced non-linearity captured in the trained autoencoder. The LTR thus enables practitioners in turbulent flow modelling to determine a priori whether non-linear compression is worthwhile, avoiding the substantial computational cost of autoencoder architecture search and hyperparameter tuning in cases where POD already suffices.

infographic.key_insight: The local tangent residual (LTR) estimates whether nonlinear compression can outperform POD before training an autoencoder.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LTR can guide reduced-order modelling choices for turbulent flows, helping avoid costly autoencoder searches when POD is sufficient.
method: Estimate nonlinear compression potential from local data geometry using LTR, without model training or a threshold parameter.
Compare LTR trends with autoencoder compression performance.
Quantify trained-decoder nonlinearity using decoder linearisation error (DLE) relative to a linearised surrogate.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two vortex street cases and a turbulent wind-turbine wake, LTR reproduced dominant autoencoder compression trends, with large nonlinear potential corroborated by large DLE.
infographic.watch_item: Validation covers three flow cases; generalisation to other turbulent regimes and datasets remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: A Priori Estimation of the Non-Linear Compression Potential and Quantification of Autoencoder Non-Linearity in Turbulent Flows

title: Thermosolutal Marangoni instabilities in a weakly viscoelastic falling film with soluble surfactant
authors: Sanghasri Mukhopadhyay, Severine Millet, Bastien Di Pierro, Asim Mukhopadhyay
abstract: We examine the linear stability and nonlinear evolution of a heated falling film containing a soluble surfactant and a weakly viscoelastic liquid. The stress response is described by the short-memory Walters model, while surface tension depends on temperature and surface concentration. An Orr--Sommerfeld analysis and its long-wave limit determine how elastic memory and the two Marangoni stresses enter the instability threshold. A five-field weighted-residual model is then derived to describe finite-amplitude disturbances. The bulk and surface transport equations are written with compatible fluxes, which conserve their combined projected surfactant inventory in a periodic domain. The numerical examples show that solutal Marangoni stress suppresses disturbance growth and reduces the amplitude of the nonlinear waves. Thermal Marangoni stress increases the maximum growth rate, although its effect on the width of the unstable wavenumber band is different. Elastic memory changes both the onset and the finite-wavelength response. The nonlinear profiles develop a main hump and capillary ripples, accompanied by variations in bulk concentration, surface concentration, and interfacial temperature. These results describe the competition between thermocapillary forcing, surfactant redistribution and elastic stress within the retained long-wave model. The larger elastic parameters are interpreted as formal predictions of the truncated constitutive equations, rather than as a controlled extension to strongly elastic flow.

infographic.key_insight: Solutal Marangoni stress stabilizes the falling film, thermal Marangoni stress increases peak disturbance growth, and elastic memory modifies instability onset and finite-wavelength behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These competing effects can inform strategies for controlling wave growth in heated, surfactant-containing viscoelastic film processes.
method: Orr–Sommerfeld stability analysis and long-wave limit.
Five-field weighted-residual model for nonlinear evolution.
Compatible bulk–surface fluxes conserving total projected surfactant inventory in periodic domains.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical examples show reduced growth and nonlinear wave amplitude with solutal Marangoni stress, alongside hump-and-ripple profiles with coupled concentration and temperature variations.
infographic.watch_item: Large-elasticity results are formal predictions of the truncated short-memory model, not controlled predictions for strongly elastic flow.
infographic.paper_title: Thermosolutal Marangoni instabilities in a weakly viscoelastic falling film with soluble surfactant

title: Theoretical progress on regularized lattice Boltzmann collision models on weakly incompressible and compressible thermal flows
authors: Xuhui Li, Xiaowen Shan, Wenyang Duan
abstract: Numerical stability has long constrained the application of lattice Boltzmann methods to high-Reynolds-number and high-Mach-number flows. Improving the stability and accuracy of collision models has therefore remained a major challenge for nearly three decades. Regularized collision models constitute an important class of lattice Boltzmann collision models and have recently undergone substantial theoretical development. They are now widely used for high-Reynolds-number turbulence, high-Mach-number compressible flow and aeroacoustics. This article systematically reviews their development and establishes a unified theoretical framework that clarifies the relationships among the principal formulations. The analysis identifies the underlying principle of the regularized multiple-relaxation collision model: higher-order kinetic moments that cannot be represented by the discrete lattice are rapidly relaxed in a coordinate-independent, self-similar moment space, thereby preventing spurious modes from contaminating the hydrodynamic equations.

infographic.key_insight: A unified theory explains how regularized lattice Boltzmann collision models rapidly relax lattice-unresolvable higher-order kinetic moments to prevent spurious contamination of hydrodynamic equations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These models support simulations of high-Reynolds-number turbulence, high-Mach-number compressible flows, and aeroacoustics, where numerical stability is a major constraint.
method: Review the theoretical development of regularized collision models.
Unify principal formulations and clarify their relationships.
Explain rapid relaxation in a coordinate-independent, self-similar moment space.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical synthesis but provides no quantitative benchmarks, datasets, or stability and accuracy comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: Stability and accuracy gains should be verified for the chosen lattice and flow regime rather than assumed from the theoretical framework.
infographic.paper_title: Theoretical progress on regularized lattice Boltzmann collision models on weakly incompressible and compressible thermal flows

title: Energy cascades in atmospheric moist convection
authors: Paweł Jędrejko, Marta Wacławczyk, Benjamin Luce, Szymon P. Malinowski, Jakub Nowak, J. Christos Vassilicos
abstract: We analyze scale-by-scale budgets of velocity and buoyancy second-order structure functions using Large Eddy Simulation of the BOMEX trade-wind cumulus layer. The simulation utilizes a $10\,\mathrm{m}$ grid resolution under the anelastic approximation, incorporating moist thermodynamics to capture phase changes. The analysis of derived turbulence kinetic energy (TKE) and turbulence potential energy (TPE) budgets reveals four regions of distinct turbulence dynamics. For three of these regions, approximate balances holding over wide range of length scales are identified, highlighting the importance of interspace and pressure transport. Above the lifting condensation level ($\approx 800\,\mathrm{m}$), phase changes introduce forcing across all resolved scales, leading to an inverse TPE cascade spanning all scales. The TKE, inter-scale transfer is inverse above the vertical velocity integral length scale but below the horizontal velocity scale. In the upper cloud layer ($>1400\,\mathrm{m}$), forward inter-scale transfers are recovered despite ongoing phase changes. A phenomenological interpretation of these features, referring to the different formation stages of convective updrafts, is also proposed. Finally, 1D horizontal subsamples from the simulation show good agreement with recent airborne measurements, validating the numerical framework and confirming the departure of moist convective turbulence from standard energy cascade models.

infographic.key_insight: Moist convection produces height- and scale-dependent energy transfers, including an inverse potential-energy cascade above cloud base and renewed forward transfers in the upper cloud layer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These findings can inform turbulence closures for cloud-resolving and weather models by highlighting phase-change forcing and transport effects absent from standard cascade assumptions.
method: Large Eddy Simulation of BOMEX trade-wind cumulus at 10 m grid resolution.
Anelastic dynamics with moist thermodynamics and phase changes.
Scale-by-scale velocity and buoyancy structure-function budgets to diagnose kinetic- and potential-energy transfers.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulation identifies four dynamical regions, and 1D horizontal subsamples agree well with recent airborne measurements.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from one simulated trade-wind cumulus case, so generalization to other cloud regimes and unresolved scales requires further testing.
infographic.paper_title: Energy cascades in atmospheric moist convection

title: Dynamic Interpolation and Higher-Order Turbulence Scales in 3D Navier-Stokes Flows
authors: Moses Patson Phiri, Zoran Grujić
abstract: We investigate the three-dimensional unforced Navier-Stokes equations through the interaction between spatial analyticity and the geometric sparseness of regions of intense fluid activity (i.e., regions where the fluid's motion varies sharply). Interpreting higher-order derivative ratios as turbulence scales, we introduce time-weighted bridge inequalities that quantify the relationship between lower- and higher-order derivative norms. The time weights give the derivative ratios greater flexibility while ensuring that the resulting lower bound on the radius of analyticity dominates the sparseness scale of the super-level sets, indicating that the flow has entered the dissipation regime. Combining this scale comparison with a harmonic-measure maximum principle on one-dimensional sparse sets yields a contraction in the relevant derivative norm, thereby excluding a class of strongly turbulent blow-up scenarios. Consequently, the strong solution extends analytically beyond the candidate blow-up time.

infographic.key_insight: Time-weighted inequalities linking derivative norms identify conditions under which analyticity dominates intense-flow sparseness, excluding a class of strongly turbulent blow-up scenarios.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Higher-order derivative ratios offer a mathematical framework for interpreting turbulence scales and the onset of dissipation in three-dimensional flows.
method: Introduce time-weighted bridge inequalities between lower- and higher-order derivative norms.
Compare the analyticity radius with the sparseness scale of intense-flow regions.
Apply a harmonic-measure maximum principle to obtain norm contraction and analytic continuation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical regularity result for unforced 3D Navier–Stokes flows, with no numerical simulations or experimental validation described.
infographic.watch_item: The result excludes a specific class of blow-up scenarios under the stated scale conditions; it does not establish unconditional global regularity.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamic Interpolation and Higher-Order Turbulence Scales in 3D Navier-Stokes Flows
